title: Break one row off a chocolate bar by hand, leaving the rest in one piece
instruction: Break one row of three pieces off one end of the chocolate bar, keeping the other nine pieces together in one piece. Leave both on the plate.
context: Snapping a row or a square off a chocolate bar by hand is something most people have done. A bar's grooves are all equally weak, so where the hands hold it and bend it decides which groove breaks: held at the two ends, a bar breaks wherever it is weakest, often in the middle.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y left, heights above the table. A white ceramic dinner plate (27 cm across, 2 cm tall, 600 g, loose) centred at x 30, y 3.6, so the groove next to the bar's right end row lies on the midline between the arms. On it, a standard 1.55 oz (43 g) milk chocolate bar of 12 pieces in 4 rows of 3, lying flat, embossed side up, its long axis along y, centred on the plate. Draft size until a bought bar is measured: 14.5 x 5.7 cm, 0.7 cm thick.
scoring: A groove breaks once it bends past 1.5 degrees (its share of 0.12 N m) or its two pieces come more than 1.5 mm or 4 degrees apart, and stays broken; pieces joined by unbroken grooves make one part. 1.0: exactly two parts, an end row of three and the other nine, every piece on the plate and still, both grippers more than 1 cm away, held 1 s. 0.75: that break, with a gripper still near or a piece moving. 0.5: an end row is off, but the other nine are in two or more parts. 0.25: broken, but no end row off on its own. 0.0: unbroken, or any piece off the plate.
reset_notes: A new bar for every real trial, at 20-22 C, unwrapped just before the trial; wipe the gripper pads with a dry cloth after each trial.
fidelity: Pieces are rigid blocks at 10x real mass (solver stability), joined at each groove by a hinge along it, sprung so its share of the groove's strength (0.12 N m, draft until measured) bends it 1.5 degrees; the task breaks it past that bend. Twisting or in-plane bending doesn't break a groove; chocolate can't crack off a groove, crush or melt. Pieces drawn in two shades so grooves show. Plate is a flat disc; one friction.
